entities.name: Arab Socialist Union
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Arab Socialist Union (ASU, الاتحاد الاشتراكي العربي, Al-Ittihad al-Ishtiraki al-Arabi), founded by Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser in 1962 as Egypt's sole ruling party — was the mass political organization of Nasserist Egypt's socialist state, designed to mobilize popular support for Nasser's Arab socialist revolution, express his pan-Arab nationalist ideology, and organize political participation within Egypt's one-party authoritarian system, serving until Anwar Sadat's subsequent restructuring.

Nasser's ASU was part of his broader vision of 'Arab socialism' — a non-communist but strongly state-interventionist economic system combined with pan-Arab nationalism and anti-imperialism. The ASU replaced earlier political organizations (the Liberation Rally, the National Union) that had proved inadequate as mass mobilization vehicles, and was modeled partly on the FLN in Algeria and the Ba'ath Party in Syria and Iraq, though Nasser's Egypt never successfully merged with either Ba'athist country despite the brief United Arab Republic experience (1958-1961).

Nasser's 1967 defeat in the Six-Day War severely damaged his political authority despite his nominal survival in power until his death in 1970. After Nasser's death, Sadat gradually dismantled the ASU structure: in 1976, he reorganized the ASU into three 'platforms' (left, center, right), then in 1978 dissolved the ASU and created the National Democratic Party, initiating Egypt's controlled multi-party system that persisted until the 2011 Egyptian Revolution.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Arab Socialist Union — Nasser's mass party for Egypt's Arab socialist revolution, destroyed by the 1967 defeat — is historically significant as the institutional expression of Nasserism, one of the 20th century's most influential Arab political ideologies.
